result:
Use OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code with PKCE against an OIDC provider, short-lived access tokens, and rotating refresh tokens tied to a per-device session record on the server. Everything else hangs off that session record.

**Sign-in:** open the provider in the system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS, Custom Tabs on Android), never an embedded webview, and ship no client secret in the app. Offer passkeys first, with password plus MFA as the fallback. On success the server creates a session row (user, device name, created, last used) and issues the token pair.

**Token lifetime and refresh:** the access token is a JWT valid for 15 minutes, carrying the session ID. The refresh token is opaque, stored hashed on the server, and valid for 30 days idle and 90 days absolute. Every refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; a replayed old token revokes the whole session, since it signals theft. Allow a grace window of a few seconds so a retry after a dropped response doesn't trip this, and have the app make only one refresh call at a time. Store tokens in the Keychain or Keystore as this-device-only, so they are excluded from backups.

**Logout:** the app calls a revoke endpoint that deletes the session, then wipes local tokens and unregisters its push token. The API checks the session ID against a cached revoked-sessions set, so logout takes effect immediately rather than when the access token expires.

**Lost phone:** the user signs in on the web or another device, sees their session list, and revokes that device, which uses the same revoke path. A password change revokes all sessions. To limit what a thief can do before that, gate the refresh token behind biometrics or the device passcode, and require fresh authentication for sensitive actions such as changing email or making payments.

Because the lost phone is often also the MFA device, issue recovery codes at enrollment and use synced passkeys. Otherwise revoking the device also locks the user out.
